title: Hacking Ethics & Law
summary: The firm line between learning and breaking the law.

pages.title: Permission is everything
pages.body:
The techniques used by ethical hackers and criminals are often identical. The only difference: permission.

- White hat: tests systems with written permission and reports findings
- Black hat: breaks in without permission for gain or damage
- Grey hat: breaks in without permission even with "good" intentions, still illegal

Without permission, "just testing" is still an attack.
pages.tip: A locksmith opening a door because the owner called is working. One opening doors uninvited is a burglar.

pages.title: The law in Indonesia
pages.body:
Indonesia's ITE Law regulates illegal access to electronic systems. Broadly, it prohibits:
- Accessing someone else's computer or system without right
- Breaching or bypassing security systems
- Altering, damaging, or moving others' data without right
- Disrupting a system so it can't work normally

Penalties include prison and fines. The Personal Data Protection Law also covers misuse of personal data. Most countries have similar laws.

This is a general overview, not legal advice.
pages.tip: Traffic laws apply even on empty roads. Other people's systems are protected even when their security is weak.

pages.title: Legal paths to grow
pages.body:
The good news: there are many legal ways to practice and even get paid:
- Practice labs: TryHackMe, Hack The Box, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, DVWA
- CTF competitions for students
- Bug bounties: official company programs that pay for vulnerability reports, with clear rules
- Responsible disclosure: if you stumble on a flaw, report it to the owner without exploiting or sharing it

A clean reputation is career capital in cyber security.
pages.tip: Want to be a great boxer? Train at the gym, not by punching people in the street.

quiz.prompt: The main difference between an ethical hacker and a criminal is...
quiz.explanation: The techniques can be identical; permission decides legality.

quiz.prompt: Casually testing your campus site's login without permission is...
quiz.explanation: Access without right is still a violation, whatever the intent.

quiz.prompt: The Indonesian law covering illegal access to electronic systems is the...
quiz.explanation: The ITE Law covers illegal access, data tampering, and system disruption.

quiz.prompt: You stumble on a flaw in an online store app. Best step?
options: Report it to the owner without exploiting it
quiz.explanation: Responsible disclosure protects users and yourself.

quiz.prompt: Which is a legal place to practice?
quiz.explanation: Labs like TryHackMe are built to be attacked legally.

title: Recon & OSINT
summary: Gathering information from open sources, and protecting your own trail.

pages.title: Recon: the first phase
pages.body:
Before testing a system, pentesters gather information. This phase is called reconnaissance (recon).

- Passive: only reading public info without touching the target, e.g. DNS records, the official site, job postings
- Active: interacting directly, e.g. port scanning. This requires permission

The better the recon, the more focused the testing.
pages.tip: Recon is like surveying a site before renovating: measure first, then demolish.

pages.title: OSINT: open source intelligence
pages.body:
OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) is info from public sources:
- Search engines and web archives
- Social media and professional profiles
- DNS records and domain registration data
- Photo metadata (GPS location, camera model)
- Leaked data already circulating publicly

OSINT is used by journalists, researchers, security teams, and sadly scammers too. From a few posts, someone can learn a person's workplace, routine, even address.
pages.tip: OSINT is piecing old newspaper clippings into a full story. Each clipping is public, but together they can be very personal.

pages.title: Ethical limits and protecting yourself
pages.body:
OSINT ethics:
- Use it to assess risk for organizations you're authorized to test, or to audit your own footprint
- Never use it for stalking, doxxing, or tracking people

Check your own trail:
- Search your name and phone number
- Check whether your email appeared in breaches at haveibeenpwned.com
- Strip location metadata before sending photos (many chat apps do it automatically, but "document" files often don't)
- Tidy the public info on your profiles
pages.tip: Before others inspect your house, walk around it yourself and close any open windows.

quiz.prompt: Passive recon means...
options: Gathering public info without touching the target
quiz.explanation: Passive recon only reads open sources.

quiz.prompt: OSINT is...
quiz.explanation: Open Source Intelligence = intelligence from public sources.

quiz.prompt: Photo metadata can leak...
options: The GPS location where it was taken
quiz.explanation: Phone photos often store GPS coordinates in metadata.

quiz.prompt: Which use of OSINT is NOT ethical?
options: Assessing a company's risk with permission
quiz.explanation: Doxxing harms people and can be illegal.

quiz.prompt: Which site checks whether your email was in a breach?
quiz.explanation: Have I Been Pwned indexes public breach data for checking.

title: Reading Logs & Incident Response
summary: How security teams spot attacks, and what they do next.

pages.title: Logs are a system's CCTV
pages.body:
Almost every system records activity in logs: who logged in, when, from which IP, what was requested, and the result.

A sample web log line:
203.0.113.7 - [24/Nov 21:03] "POST /login" 401

Meaning: IP 203.0.113.7 tried to log in and failed (401). One line is normal. A thousand similar lines in five minutes is a story.

Try grep in the Terminal Simulator to practice finding patterns.
pages.tip: Logs are a building's guest book and CCTV footage. Usually boring, until something happens.

pages.title: Suspicious patterns
pages.body:
What analysts (blue team / SOC) usually hunt for:
- Many failed logins then one success: a password guess that finally worked
- Logins from unusual countries or hours
- Requests with odd patterns like ' OR 1=1 or <script>
- Huge traffic spikes from many IPs: possibly DDoS
- A regular account suddenly accessing admin data

Tools called SIEMs gather logs from many systems and raise alerts automatically.
pages.tip: A good guard doesn't watch every recording, but knows which moments to replay.

pages.title: Incident response steps
pages.body:
When an incident happens, teams follow a common flow:
1. Preparation: have a plan, contacts, and backups before anything happens
2. Detection & analysis: confirm it's real and how wide it is
3. Containment: isolate affected systems so it doesn't spread
4. Eradication: remove the attacker's access and patch the flaw
5. Recovery: restore services from clean backups
6. Lessons learned: record what to improve so it doesn't recur

Personal accounts work the same way: lock (change password), check damage, recover, and harden (2FA).
pages.tip: Like firefighting: contain the fire so it doesn't spread, find the cause, repair, then install better alarms.

quiz.prompt: The log line "POST /login" 401 means...
quiz.explanation: 401 = authentication failed.

quiz.prompt: Hundreds of failed logins then one success from the same IP suggests...
options: A password guess that finally worked
quiz.explanation: A successful brute-force pattern needs immediate follow-up.

quiz.prompt: A SIEM is used to...
options: Collect logs and raise automatic alerts
quiz.explanation: A SIEM unifies logs from many systems for analysis.

quiz.prompt: The step after detection that stops an incident from spreading is...
quiz.explanation: Containment limits damage before eradication.

quiz.prompt: Your social media account was hijacked. The right order?
options: Make a new account and forget it
Secure it (change password, sign out sessions), check damage, recover, enable 2FA
Wait for the hijacker to get bored
quiz.explanation: The incident response flow applies to personal accounts too.

title: CTF & Career Paths
summary: How to practice with direction, and the roles in cyber security.

pages.title: CTF: learning by playing
pages.body:
Capture The Flag (CTF) competitions are about finding "flags", secret text hidden in challenges. Typical categories:
- Web: web app flaws
- Crypto: breaking ciphers
- Forensics: analyzing files, images, or network captures
- Reverse engineering: dissecting programs
- OSINT and misc

You've already tried a mini version in this app. The flags use the same format: CIPHER{...}.
pages.tip: A CTF is a digital escape room: each clue opens the next door.

pages.title: Roles in cyber security
pages.body:
Cyber security is broad, not just "hackers":
- Red team / pentester: tests systems by attacking them, with permission
- Blue team / SOC analyst: monitors, detects, and responds to attacks
- Security engineer: builds secure systems and infrastructure
- AppSec: secures application code, great for people who like coding
- GRC: policy, audits, and compliance
- Digital forensics: investigates evidence after incidents

Many people start in IT support, networking, or development, then move into security.
pages.tip: Like a hospital: surgeons, on-call doctors, pharmacists, management. All essential.

pages.title: Your next learning plan
pages.body:
After Cipher, a sensible order:
1. Strengthen the basics: networking, Linux, and one scripting language (Python or Bash)
2. Guided practice: TryHackMe beginner paths, or PortSwigger Academy for web
3. Join beginner CTFs, solo or with friends, and write up your solutions
4. Build a portfolio: log completed labs on GitHub or a blog
5. An entry-level certification if you need it for jobs, e.g. CompTIA Security+ or similar

30 consistent minutes a day beats a weekly marathon.
pages.tip: Learning cyber security is like climbing a mountain: no need to run, just don't stop walking.

quiz.prompt: In a CTF, a "flag" is...
options: Secret text you need to find
quiz.explanation: Finding the flag proves you solved the challenge.

quiz.prompt: The CTF category about dissecting programs is...
quiz.explanation: Reverse engineering analyzes how programs work without source code.

quiz.prompt: The role that monitors and responds to attacks is...
quiz.explanation: The blue team defends; the red team tests by attacking.

quiz.prompt: For people who love coding, the most related security role is...
quiz.explanation: AppSec focuses on securing code and applications.

quiz.prompt: The most effective study habit according to this module?
quiz.explanation: Regular practice makes knowledge stick longer.
